subject: biology
subTopic: The Eye, Ear and Other Receptors

questions.content: What is a receptor in the nervous system?
options: A cell or organ that detects a stimulus
A muscle that produces a response
A neurone that carries messages to the brain only
questions.explanation: Receptors detect stimuli such as light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals. Muscles and glands are effectors.

questions.content: Which part of the eye contains the light-sensitive cells?
questions.explanation: The retina contains rod and cone cells that detect light. The cornea and lens refract light and the iris controls the pupil size.

questions.content: Which part of the ear contains the cochlea?
questions.explanation: The cochlea is in the inner ear. It converts vibrations into nerve impulses.

questions.content: Which structure of the eye controls the amount of light entering by changing the size of the pupil?
questions.explanation: The muscles of the iris make the pupil larger or smaller. The retina detects light and the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain.

questions.content: Which sense organ contains receptors that detect chemicals in the air?
questions.explanation: The nose has chemical receptors that detect smell. The tongue has chemical receptors for taste.

questions.content: In bright light, what happens to the pupil and why?
options: It gets smaller to protect the retina from too much light
It gets larger to let more light in
It moves to the side of the eye
questions.explanation: Circular muscles in the iris contract, making the pupil smaller. This stops damage to the retina.

questions.content: Which sequence correctly shows the path of light entering the eye?
questions.explanation: Light is refracted by the cornea, passes through the pupil, is focused by the lens and lands on the retina.

questions.content: When looking at a close object, what happens to the lens?
questions.explanation: For near objects, ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes fatter, which bends light more strongly.

questions.content: Which sequence correctly shows how sound passes through the ear?
options: Ear drum → ossicles → cochlea → auditory nerve
Cochlea → ossicles → ear drum → auditory nerve
Ossicles → auditory nerve → ear drum → cochlea
Ear drum → cochlea → ossicles → auditory nerve
questions.explanation: Sound makes the ear drum vibrate, the ossicles (three small bones) pass and amplify vibrations to the cochlea, which sends impulses along the auditory nerve.

questions.content: Rod cells and cone cells differ because:
options: Rods work in dim light; cones detect colour in bright light
Rods detect colour; cones work in dim light
Rods are in the lens; cones are in the cornea
questions.explanation: Rods are sensitive in dim light but do not detect colour. Cones need brighter light and give colour vision.

questions.content: Alicia has short-sightedness (myopia). She can see near objects clearly but distant objects look blurred. What is the likely cause?
options: Light from distant objects is focused in front of the retina
Light from distant objects is focused behind the retina
questions.explanation: In myopia the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong, so light from far away focuses in front of the retina. A concave (diverging) lens corrects it.

questions.content: A person walks from bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens to the pupil over the next few seconds?
questions.explanation: Radial muscles of the iris contract and circular muscles relax, making the pupil wider to let in more light.

questions.content: Skin contains receptors that detect which stimuli?
questions.explanation: The skin has a range of receptors for touch, pressure, heat, cold and pain.

questions.content: Mei Ling stands near a loud concert speaker for hours. Later she finds quiet sounds hard to hear. Which explanation is best?
options: Loud sound can damage the sensory hair cells in the cochlea
Loud sound makes the ear drum thicker
questions.explanation: The hair cells in the cochlea detect vibrations. Very loud noise can damage them permanently, causing hearing loss.

questions.content: Why can people not see well in dim light at the edges of their vision and see few colours at night?
options: Rods work in dim light but do not detect colour, and cones need brighter light
Cones work best in dim light
The lens turns black at night
questions.explanation: At night mostly rod cells are working. They cannot tell colours apart, so the world appears in shades of grey.

questions.content: A student tests a volunteer's pupil size as a torch is shone towards the eye. Pupil diameter: before 7 mm, after 3 mm. What is the best conclusion?
options: The pupil reflex reduced light entering the eye, which protects the retina
questions.explanation: The pupil decreased from 7 mm to 3 mm, a response to bright light that limits light reaching the retina. The data does not show changes in the lens or cornea.

questions.content: A person has damage to the optic nerve but a healthy eye. Which effect is most likely?
options: Light is focused normally but impulses cannot reach the brain, so vision is lost or reduced
The lens cannot change shape but vision is normal
questions.explanation: The retina can detect light, but the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain. Without it, the brain cannot form the image.

questions.content: Diego is given 'receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector' as a pathway. Which description of the ear's role fits this list correctly?
options: The cochlea hair cells are receptors; the auditory nerve carries impulses to the brain
The ear drum is the motor neurone
The outer ear is the relay neurone
questions.explanation: The sensory hair cells in the cochlea are the receptors and the auditory nerve is made of sensory neurones. The ossicles and ear drum are not neurones or effectors.

note:
Our senses let us detect changes in the environment. A **stimulus** is a change that can be detected, and a **receptor** is a cell or organ that detects it. Receptors turn the stimulus into nerve impulses, which travel to the brain, where a response is decided. Muscles and glands that carry out the response are called **effectors**.

## The eye
Light enters the eye and is bent (refracted) so that it forms a sharp image on the retina.
- **Cornea:** transparent front surface that does most of the bending of light.
- **Iris:** coloured ring of muscle that controls pupil size.
- **Pupil:** hole in the iris where light enters.
- **Lens:** changes shape to fine-focus light.
- **Retina:** layer at the back containing **rods** (work in dim light, no colour) and **cones** (colour, need bright light).
- **Optic nerve:** carries impulses to the brain.

### Pupil reflex
In bright light, circular muscles of the iris contract and the pupil gets smaller, protecting the retina. In dim light, radial muscles contract and the pupil gets larger to let more light in.

### Focusing
To see a **near** object, ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes thicker and rounder. To see a **distant** object, ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tighten and the lens becomes thinner. In short-sightedness, distant objects are focused in front of the retina and a concave lens corrects it. In long-sightedness, near objects are focused behind the retina and a convex lens corrects it.

## The ear
The ear detects sound and also helps with balance.
- **Pinna** collects sound.
- **Ear drum** vibrates.
- **Ossicles** (three small bones) pass the vibrations on and make them stronger.
- **Cochlea** contains hair cells that turn vibrations into nerve impulses.
- **Auditory nerve** carries impulses to the brain.
The semicircular canals contain receptors that detect head movement and help balance. Very loud noise can permanently damage the hair cells.

## Other receptors
- Skin: touch, pressure, temperature and pain.
- Nose: chemicals in the air (smell).
- Tongue: chemicals in food (taste: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami).

## Common mistakes
- Saying the lens does all the bending of light. The cornea does most of it.
- Mixing up which muscles do what when the pupil changes. Link size to light: bright light, small pupil.
- Forgetting that the receptor is the cell (for example rod or hair cell) not the whole organ.

## How this is examined
Questions often give a scenario, such as a person moving from sunshine into a dark cinema or an investigation of pupil size. You may be asked to label or describe the path of light or sound, explain a response, interpret data in a short table described in words, or evaluate how reliable an investigation is.

Exam tip: When explaining the pupil reflex, state the stimulus, the receptor or effector involved and the result (for example 'bright light, iris muscles contract, pupil smaller, less light reaches the retina').

flashcards.back: A stimulus is a change in the environment. A receptor is a cell or organ that detects it.
Contains rod and cone cells (light receptors) that send impulses along the optic nerve to the brain.
Rods: work in dim light, no colour. Cones: detect colour, need bright light.
Circular iris muscles contract, pupil gets smaller, protecting the retina.

flashcards.front: Lens when focusing on a near object
flashcards.back: Ciliary muscles contract, ligaments slacken, lens becomes thicker and rounder.

flashcards.front: Path of sound through the ear
flashcards.back: Pinna, ear canal, ear drum, ossicles, cochlea (hair cells), auditory nerve, brain.
Three small bones that pass on and amplify vibrations from the ear drum to the cochlea.
Distant objects focus in front of the retina. Corrected by a concave (diverging) lens.
Contain receptors that detect head movement and help with balance.

subject: biology

questions.content: What is a reflex action?
options: A fast, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought
A slow response that needs thinking
A response that only happens during sleep
A learned skill such as riding a bike
questions.explanation: Reflexes are quick, automatic and protective. They do not need the conscious part of the brain.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of a reflex action?
options: Blinking when something flies towards your eye
Choosing what to eat for lunch
questions.explanation: Blinking is a quick protective reflex. The other actions are voluntary.

questions.content: Which type of neurone carries impulses from a receptor to the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Sensory neurones carry impulses towards the CNS. Motor neurones carry impulses to effectors.

questions.content: Which two organs make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
questions.explanation: The CNS is made of the brain and spinal cord.

questions.content: What is an effector?
options: A muscle or gland that carries out a response
questions.explanation: Muscles contract and glands secrete in response to impulses. They are effectors.

questions.content: Which sequence shows the correct order of a reflex arc?
options: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response
Stimulus → effector → relay neurone → receptor → response
Receptor → motor neurone → sensory neurone → effector
Stimulus → relay neurone → receptor → sensory neurone → response
questions.explanation: A reflex arc begins with the stimulus detected by a receptor and ends with an effector producing a response, with sensory, relay and motor neurones between.

questions.content: Where is the relay neurone found in a spinal reflex?
questions.explanation: The relay neurone is within the CNS (spinal cord) and connects sensory to motor neurones.

questions.content: A synapse is:
options: A tiny gap between two neurones where chemicals carry the signal across
A thick fatty layer around an axon
A muscle that moves a limb
questions.explanation: At a synapse the impulse is carried across the gap by neurotransmitter chemicals, which bind to receptors on the next neurone.

questions.content: Why are reflex actions useful for survival?
options: They are very fast, so they protect the body from harm
questions.explanation: By bypassing conscious thought the response is faster. This helps avoid injury, for example pulling a hand away from heat.

questions.content: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a voluntary action from a reflex?
options: A voluntary action involves the conscious part of the brain and is slower
A voluntary action does not use neurones
A reflex action always involves the brain's thinking areas
questions.explanation: Voluntary actions are decided by the brain. Reflexes pass through the spinal cord (or lower brain) without needing conscious decisions.

questions.content: Why does the myelin sheath around some neurones speed up impulses?
options: It insulates the axon so impulses travel faster
questions.explanation: The fatty myelin sheath insulates the axon and allows the impulse to jump along it, increasing speed.

questions.content: Pavlov-style conditioning: a dog hears a bell each time food arrives and eventually salivates at the bell alone. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The dog has learned to link the bell with food. Salivating for food is a natural reflex, but salivating to a bell is learned.

questions.content: A newborn baby grasps a finger placed in its palm. This type of behaviour is best described as:
questions.explanation: Newborn babies show reflexes, such as grasping and sucking, which they did not need to learn.

questions.content: Rashid touches a hot pan and his hand pulls away before he feels pain. Which explanation is best?
options: The reflex arc goes through the spinal cord, so the response happens before the brain processes the pain
The brain decides to move the hand before the stimulus
The relay neurone is in the hand
questions.explanation: The signal passes via the spinal cord to the effector (muscle), producing a quick response. Impulses also travel to the brain afterwards, which is when pain is felt.

questions.content: A drug blocks the receptors on the post-synaptic neurone at synapses. What is the most likely effect on a reflex?
options: The reflex would be slowed or blocked because the signal cannot cross the synapse
No effect, because impulses can jump across the gap electrically
The sensory neurone would become a motor neurone
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters need receptors to start a new impulse. If receptors are blocked, transmission across the synapse fails.

questions.content: In an experiment a student drops a ruler and a volunteer catches it. The ruler falls 12 cm in trial 1, 10 cm in trial 2 and 8 cm in trial 3 (same volunteer, practising). Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Reaction time improved with practice, which suggests catching is partly a learned, voluntary response
Catching a ruler is a true reflex, so practice has no effect
questions.explanation: Shorter fall distance means faster reaction. Practice improved it, which a true reflex would not do. More trials and more volunteers would increase reliability.

questions.content: Which statement best compares nervous and hormonal communication?
options: Nervous responses are quick and short-lived; hormonal responses are slower and last longer
Nervous responses are slower and last longer
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses are electrical and fast. Hormones travel in the blood so effects are slower but often longer-lasting.

questions.content: A scientist records that a person with spinal cord damage in the lower back can still jerk the knee when the tendon is tapped but cannot feel the tap. What does this suggest?
options: The reflex arc is below the damage, but impulses cannot reach the brain to give a sensation
The brain controls the knee jerk
questions.explanation: A knee-jerk reflex arc is processed in the spinal cord. Damage higher up stops signals reaching the brain, so the person feels nothing even though the reflex still happens. This depends on where the damage is.

note:
Behaviour is how an organism responds to its environment. Some behaviours are automatic and inborn, while others are learned. Understanding the nervous system pathway behind a reflex helps explain how organisms react quickly to danger.

## The nervous system
The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the brain and spinal cord. The **peripheral nervous system** is the nerves that connect the rest of the body to the CNS. Information travels as electrical impulses along neurones.
- **Sensory neurones** carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.
- **Relay neurones** are inside the CNS and connect sensory to motor neurones.
- **Motor neurones** carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.
Neurones can be covered in a fatty **myelin sheath** that insulates them and speeds up the impulse.

## Synapses
Neurones do not touch. At a **synapse** there is a tiny gap. The impulse in one neurone triggers the release of **neurotransmitter** chemicals, which diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, starting a new impulse. Synapses make sure impulses travel in one direction only.

## The reflex arc
A **reflex** is a fast, automatic, protective response. The pathway is called the **reflex arc**:
- stimulus
- receptor
- sensory neurone
- relay neurone (in the spinal cord)
- motor neurone
- effector (muscle or gland)
- response.
Because the pathway is short and does not wait for the conscious brain, the response is very fast. Examples include pulling a hand from a hot object, blinking, the pupil reflex and the knee jerk. Impulses also go up to the brain, which is why you feel pain slightly after you pull away.

## Voluntary and learned behaviour
A **voluntary** response is decided by the brain and is slower. Behaviour can be **innate** (inborn, such as a baby's grasp reflex) or **learned**. In conditioning, an animal links a new stimulus to an old reflex, for example a dog that salivates at a bell after the bell has repeatedly been paired with food. Practice can also improve skills, such as catching a ball.

## Nervous vs hormonal control
Nervous responses use electrical impulses: fast and short-lived. Hormonal responses use chemicals in the blood: slower but longer-lasting.

## Common mistakes
- Writing that the brain is always part of a reflex arc. For many reflexes the spinal cord is the coordinator.
- Mixing the order of sensory and motor neurones.
- Saying neurones touch at a synapse. There is a gap.

## How this is examined
Typical items give a short scenario, such as a hand touching a hot object or a reaction time test using a dropped ruler, and ask you to order the arc, explain why it is fast, interpret results, or evaluate the reliability of an investigation (repeat trials, same conditions, several volunteers).

Exam tip: In reflex arc questions, write the full pathway in order and name each neurone type, then state why this makes the response quick.

flashcards.back: A fast, automatic, protective response that does not involve conscious thought.
Stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector, response.
Sensory carries impulses from receptors to the CNS. Motor carries impulses from the CNS to effectors.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response.
Tiny gap between neurones. Neurotransmitters diffuse across and start a new impulse in the next neurone.
Fatty layer that insulates an axon and speeds up the impulse.
Innate: inborn (e.g. a baby's grasp reflex). Learned: gained through experience or conditioning.
Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived. Hormonal: slower, in the blood, longer-lasting.
